# **Assessment of wind-farm and other bird casualties from carcasses found on a Northumbrian beach over an 11-year period**

## IAN  NEWTON[1] * and  BRIAN  LITTLE[2]

> _[1] Monks Wood Research Station ,  Abbots Ripton ,  Huntingdon ,  Cambridgeshire ,  PE28 2LS ,  U K and[2 ] AMEC Wind Energy ,  Bridge End ,  Hexham ,  Northumberland ,  NE46 4NU ,  UK_

**Capsule** For 3748 bird carcasses found on 4.7 km of shoreline, the main cause of death was starvation. Three percent of deaths were attributed to wind turbines.

**Aims** To assess the main mortality causes from bird bodies washed ashore near wind turbines built in 1993.

**Methods** Weekly searches were made for bird carcasses to ascertain causes of death. Experiments tested the efficiency of searches, longevity of carcasses, and effects of wind direction on deposition rates.

**Results** In total, 3748 bird carcasses were found, an average of 341 per year. Guillemots formed 24.3% of the total, Kittiwakes 9.7%, Herring Gulls 9.0%, Black-headed Gulls 7.4%, Great Black-backed Gulls 6.4% and Feral Pigeons 11.3%. Each year more carcasses were found in winter than in summer, with a nine-fold variation between winters. About 28.1% of carcasses were classed as starved, and 23.3% as eaten at sea (predation or scavenging). Of human-related causes, 3.3% were birds affected by fishing gear, 3.0% were oiled, 6.4% had died from collisions (including 3% with wind-turbines), the rest from minor or unidentified causes. Small passerines were probably under-represented.

**Conclusion** Allowing for bodies not found, the local wind-farm probably killed 148.5–193.5 birds per year, or 16.5–21.5 birds per turbine per year (mainly large gulls).

In this paper, we describe the numbers and species composition of bird carcasses found on a 4.7 km stretch of beach in Northumberland, northeast England, searched almost every week over an 11-year period (December 1991–November 2002). In the midst of the search area lies a small wind-farm, with nine operational turbines, potentially able to kill birds. All carcasses found on the nearby shoreline were examined to determine, as far as possible, the cause of death. The main objective was to find what proportion of the birds found dead were likely to have been killed by collision with the turbines themselves, rather than by some other causal factor. This assessment could be made separately for the various species commonly found. The turbines were operational from January 1993, which gave about 1 year of data before this date, and about 10 years subsequently. As far as we are aware, this is the first study of its kind conducted over

such a long time period, although a provisional summary account of some aspects of the work has been provided by Lawrence _et al_ . (2007). The main findings were that, in this situation, turbines caused a relatively small part of the total bird mortality recorded, and affected mainly large gulls.

## **STUDY SITE AND TURBINES**

The study was conducted at the town of Blyth, on the Northumbrian coast in northeast England (55° 7 _'_ N, 1° 30 _'_ W). At this site, nine wind turbines (individual capacity 300kW) were constructed, each with three rotor blades, mounted on conical solid-sided steel towers. Two of the turbines are on land, while seven others stretch south-eastward in a line along a rockand-concrete pier (constructed 1880), which forms the eastern side of a harbour, and provides shelter from the open sea. The towers extend in a line, about 200 m apart; each tower extends up to 30 m (hub height),

while the rotors (25 m diameter) extend from 17.5 m above ground to 42.5 m above ground. Outside the harbour, sandy beaches extend north and south. The harbour is used by a small fishing fleet and a small number of other boats, including bulk alumina freighters. It attracts many birds, notably Common Eiders _Somateria mollissima_ (up to 180 birds, as part of a larger local population) which come in to feed every day (usually by swimming) and large numbers of gulls, which increase whenever fishing boats return. In winter, a roost of gulls in the harbour reaches about 2500 Herring Gulls _Larus argentatus_ and about 500 Great Black-backed Gulls _Larus marinus_ . North of the harbour is the estuary of the River Blyth, which is a favoured feeding site for terns and other birds. About 20 other tall structures (20–30 m) occur around the harbour area, including cranes, communication masts, silos and warehouses, as well as overhead wires. About 15 km north of Blyth lies Coquet Island, and about 60 km to the north the Farne Islands, which together provide major breeding sites for many species of seabirds. At migration times, various seabirds travel offshore up or down the coast (which runs roughly north–south), while many land-birds move broadly east–west between continental Europe and Britain. Many feral pigeons nest on the buildings around the harbour, and throughout the summer thousands move up and down the coast on races or training flights. The same pier that supports the turbines also accommodates a roost of Great Cormorants _Phalacrocorax carbo_ (up to 120 birds), and at its far end a roost of Purple Sandpipers _Calidris maritima_ (up to _c._ 360 birds), while the understructure of a nearby wharf supports a large roost of Common Starlings _Sturnus vulgaris_ (up to several thousand birds). In general, therefore, the locality is fairly rich in both seabirds and land-birds.

## **METHODS**

Searches were made of the north and south beaches, the ‘alcan beach’, the estuary, the harbour itself, including the pier supporting the turbines, and the tiny storm beach composed of pebbles at the northern end of the East Pier facing the sea. Overall, this coastline totalled 3.2 km of soft, sloping shoreline where bodies were washed up, and another 1.5 km of steeper rocky shoreline, where no bodies were found. The whole 4.7 km stretch was searched over a period of up to 2 days, once each week, in most weeks during each of 11 years, from December 1991 to November 2002 inclusive. However, no counts were made in May–June 1992 and July 1993.

The beaches were narrow (80–150 m exposed between low and high tide depending on steepness), and it was possible from the walk-route along high tide-line to survey the whole area between the highest tide-lines and low water. The only bird carcasses and partcarcasses that might have been missed were any buried under freshly piled seaweed or sand. Individual small bones and feathers were ignored.

Each beach took 2–6 hours to search, depending on the numbers of carcasses present, which varied between nil and several dozens. In mid-winter, when carcass numbers were high, the searches and data gathering often occupied almost the whole daylight period. Where possible, each carcass was identified and measured (wing-length), and fresh ones were also weighed. Each carcass was also examined to ascertain the likely cause of death (see later). All found carcasses were cleared from the beach at each count to prevent re-counting on future walks. The right leg at the ankle joint was removed in order to identify any bodies that might have re-appeared on the beaches.

Depending on its condition, each carcass was placed in one of the following categories:

1.  Starved: thin, with protruding sternum; usually around two-thirds of normal weight.

2.  Diseased: obvious swellings or other external signs of disease. Because birds were not examined internally (apart from the mouth and gullet), we could not exclude the possibility that disease contributed to the deaths of some birds classed as starved.

3.  Eaten at sea: sternum and wing bones with primary feathers attached, the remainder of the carcass having been stripped of soft tissue.

4.  Eaten on land: carcass plucked and eaten on the beach, disguising the true cause of death.

5.  Killed by bird of prey. Plucked and eaten on the beach while fresh.

6.  Toxin poisoning: mostly emaciated gulls with green stain around cloaca, thought to have died of botulism poisoning; also included Kittiwakes _Rissa tridactyla_ in good physical condition but probably poisoned offshore by natural toxins.

7.  Exhausted migrants: land-birds of low weight (but not starved), but otherwise in good condition; no apparent cause of death.

8.  Apparently fallen from nest or roost above water.

9.  Suffocation: large food item stuck in throat.

10.  Drowned in net: wings set out at an angle to the body (caused by _rigor mortis_ in the net), monofilament score marks on plumage, water-filled lungs.

11.  Tangled in monofilament line or embedded hook, discarded from rod-and-line fishing.

12.  Shot: obvious gunshot wounds in an otherwise healthy-looking bird.

13.  Oiled: plumage largely or totally covered in oil.

14.  Wind-farm collision: mutilated fresh carcass or part-carcass, often with head, one or both wings missing, and broken bones, blood in body cavity and ruptured liver.

15.  Other collision: carcass complete, good condition, but with extensive bruising, often lying at the base of a building or other structure.

16.  Road casualties: birds found dead on busy road between north and south beaches.

17.  Injured birds found alive in the harbour, probably having collided with wires or other obstacles. Some lived by scavenging for long periods.

18.  Skeletal remains: bones only, apparently long at sea (skulls, sternums or pelvic girdles, identified to species by use of reference material).

19.  Unknown cause: identified to species, but long dead and well rotted.

For birds recorded as eaten at sea, it was impossible to tell whether they were killed by a predator and then eaten, or scavenged after death from some other cause. Both types of events, involving large gulls as the predators and scavengers, were witnessed during the study. In addition, carcasses washed on the beaches were fed upon by large gulls, Carrion Crows _Corvus corone_ , cats and rats, and possibly other animals, but to judge from those witnessed, remains were normally left and not carried away (see later).

## **RESULTS**

Over the 11-year period, 3748 bird bodies of at least 102 species were found on the 4.7 km of coastal search area; an average of 341 carcasses per calendar year (range 131–713) (Table  1 ). The first full year of study (1992, before the turbines became operational) gave a total of 253 carcasses, which was within the range of totals from subsequent years, but below the overall median value (334). Overall, the most frequently found species was Common Guillemot _Uria aalge,_ which formed 24.3% of the total number, most having apparently starved. Five other species each formed more than 5% of the total, namely Kittiwake _Rissa tridactyla_ (9.66%), Herring Gull (8.96%), Black-headed Gull _Larus ridibundus_ (7.41%), Great Black-backed Gull (6.37%) and Feral Pigeon _Columba livia_ (11.31%), the

six species together making 68.01% of the total. The large number of pigeons reflected the numbers nesting on buildings around the harbour. The 25 species of passerines were dominated by Starlings (2.2% of all carcasses), again probably reflecting the presence of a winter roost under the wharf. Most other passerines were found at migration times, and were classed as victims of exhaustion or gull predation; the commonest being Fieldfare _Turdus pilaris_ (1.1% of all carcasses).

Each year, many more carcasses were washed ashore in the winter months (October–March) than in the summer months (April–September) (Tables  1 &  2 ; Figure  1 ). Winter numbers varied more than nine-fold from year to year (52 in 1998–99 to 480 in 1995–96), while summer numbers varied less than four-fold from year to year (72 in 2002 to 282 in 1996). Within winters, numbers were greatest in the months of January– March, as shown for Guillemots in Table  3 .

A major ‘wreck’ of seabirds occurred on the northeast coast of Britain during a 3-week period of cold windy weather in February 1994, and this was reflected in the large numbers of seabird carcasses found in that month at Blyth (267 of 14 species). This total was by far the largest number of bodies found in any single month during the 11-year study. Most were of Guillemots (184, 68.9%) or European Shags _Phalacrocorax aristotelis_ (40, 15.0%). Other ‘incidents’ occurred in the late summers of 1995–97, but affected Kittiwakes only. The biggest at Blyth was in 1997 when more than 60 fresh Kittiwake carcasses were washed ashore, but over a wider area of northeast England several thousands were found in 1996 and 1997.

Out of 3748 carcass remains found at Blyth, some 874 specimens were washed up as wings-and-sternum, the second most important category recorded, at 23.32% of all carcasses (Table 4). On the basis of observational evidence, these were classed as victims of gull predation/scavenging, but fish and other marine creatures may have been among the consumers. Although it was impossible to judge what proportion of these had died before being eaten, both Herring and Great Blackbacked Gulls were frequently seen to chase incoming migrants, forcing them into the water, where they could be grabbed, and then eaten. Normally, the whole carcass was eaten, apart from the sternum-and-wings – the remnants that were often found on the beaches. Usually several gulls chased the same bird at once, and were also quick to attack any injured gull, even of the largest species. Brent Goose _B. bernicla_ , Great Skua _Stercorarius skua_ , Arctic Skua _S. parasiticus_ , Long-eared Owl _Asio otus_ , Eurasian Woodcock _Scolopax rusticola_ , Jack Snipe _Lymocryptes minimus_ and many others. Other species, such as Eurasian Kestrel _Falco tinnunculus_ and Merlin _F. columbarius_ , were often seen to be chased but evaded capture. In addition to the supposed gull victims, the remains of 92 other (mostly smaller) birds were found that had apparently been plucked (and presumably killed) by raptors. They included mostly passerines and waders. Likely predators were Eurasian Sparrowhawks _Accipiter nisus_ , Merlins and Peregrine Falcons _Falco peregrinus_ , all of which were frequently seen hunting along the shoreline.

Some 116 (3.09%) deaths were attributed to toxin poisoning. They included the large numbers of Kittiwakes found dead in otherwise excellent condition in the summers of 1995–97 (especially 1997). Others were found on other northeast coasts at the same time and, despite extensive veterinary and chemical analyses, no firm causal factor was ascertained. In the absence of other symptoms, these deaths were tentatively attributed to toxin poisoning, either natural from an algal bloom or man-made. Smaller numbers of Kittiwakes in similar conditions were found in the summers of 1994 and 1998. Some gull deaths were attributed to botulism, but here the evidence was more convincing, with typical symptoms of emaciation and green staining around the cloaca. Most examples were found at the south harbour roosts of Herring Gulls and Great Black-backed Gulls. Many of these birds fed at a land-fill site at Ashington, about 10 km away.

The fifth most important category of death was attributed to various human-related causes, including oil pollution (111 specimens, 2.96%); and entanglement in fishing gear, either drift nets (85 specimens, 2.27%) or lines and hooks (discarded from rod and line fishing, 33 specimens, 0.88%). Species affected by oiling and entanglement were mainly Guillemots, other auks, and divers. In addition, a total of 245 (6.53%) deaths were attributed to collisions, 114 (3.04%) with the wind turbines and 129 (3.44%) with other tall structures or

wires. Some of these corpses were found beside the buildings themselves. Despite the central position of the wind farm in the study area, it emerged as one of the least important sources of mortality among birds found on nearby beaches. In all, 114 individuals of 15 species were recorded as probably killed by turbines. This averages at 11.4 recovered birds per year of operation (from 1993) for the whole farm, and 1.3 recovered birds per turbine per year. The most-frequently recorded victims were Herring Gulls (39), Great Black-backed Gulls (36), Black-headed Gulls (7) and Common Eiders (15). These four were the commonest large species in the vicinity. Although no change in the overall collision rate occurred during the study period, 12 of the 15 Eiders were killed in the first 3 years of the study. In later years, Eiders took to swimming (rather than flying) into the harbour, probably as a result of a local change in distribution, and only three other Eider casualties were recorded in the next 8 years. During the course of the study, two gulls were actually seen to collide with a moving rotor blade, while a Northern Fulmar _Fulmarus glacialis_ hit the tower itself, and all three fell dead to the water or ground below. All three incidents occurred in conditions of mist and poor visibility. Unseen wind-farm collision deaths occurred throughout the year, but were less frequent in summer, when fewer birds were in the area than in winter.

For 590 (15.74%) specimens, a category of death could not be ascertained, because they had been long dead (557) or were skeletal (33); another 310 (8.27%) had been eaten on the beaches and 89 (2.7%) were put down to raptors kills. The remaining 228 (6.08%) deaths were attributed to a range of minor causes. Two Cormorants, a Common Eider and Great Black-backed Gull had apparently died of

## **EXPERIMENTAL ASSESSMENT OF FINDINGS**

While we see no reason for bias in the proportion of deaths attributed to different categories, we can make no claim that all carcasses washed into the search area during the study were found and recorded, or that all windfarm casualties were washed into the search area. Indeed, in conditions of strong westerly winds, many bodies are likely to have been blown out to sea, as mimicked in experiments with wooden blocks, described below.

## **Search success**

In order to test the success rate of the beach searches, 20 carcasses found locally were distributed at random by a volunteer between the high and low water marks along a 1 km stretch of study beach. This was done in the absence of the usual collector (second author), and in advance of his scheduled visit. All these corpses were discretely marked with a small bird ring placed around the outermost primary, under the primary coverts, and any other corpses were left _in situ_ . The beach was watched in the period between when the corpses were distributed and the search began, in order to check for any unusual animal or human activity which might have affected the positions of the test corpses. No disturbance was seen in this period. The following day,

19 of the 20 corpses were then found by the collector, a 95% recovery rate. Such a high recovery rate might not have been achieved on every search, but it did suggest that the majority of corpses present at search times were likely to have been found.

## **Longevity of floating corpses**

How long could fresh carcasses remain afloat before disintegrating or sinking? Two fresh Guillemot carcasses were tied on a long piece of plastic string to a floating pontoon in the harbour, and checked twice each week until they sank. They were not attacked by gulls or rats (being no longer fresh-looking), but were subject to the usual tidal changes and wash from shipping. From 24 March when the trial started, the bodies remained intact and afloat until 1 May (38 days) and 22 May (59 days) respectively. Two freshly dead Shags given the same treatment from 18 February, remained afloat until 14–20 June (at least 116 days). If carcasses on the open sea could remain afloat for similar periods and were not consumed by predators, they could travel for hundreds of kilometres before sinking or being washed ashore. This finding helped to reinforce our supposition that many of the carcasses found at Blyth could have travelled long distances.

## **Longevity of corpses on the beach**

We had no way of knowing how many carcasses might have appeared on the beach, and disappeared, between

successive weekly counts. However, in the weeks of 24–30 January and 21–27 February 1994, carcasses were inconspicuously marked as described previously, and their positions noted. The beach was then checked every day for a week to find what proportion of marked carcasses remained on the beach for a full week. The proportion that disappeared revealed the extent to which our counts might have under-estimated the total number washed ashore.

On 24 January, nine marked carcasses were placed on the beaches and three disappeared within the week (on days 4, 6 and 6), while the six others remained until days 12, 12, 25, 31, 34 and 43. On 21 February, another 70 marked carcasses were placed on the beaches, but unfortunately a major wreck of seabirds had occurred this month (see earlier), which stimulated the local RSPB staff to organise carcass collections. Only one stretch of shoreline (including the North Beach) was not covered in this way, which greatly reduced our sample size. During this week, there was also an exceptionally high tide and an unusual amount of sand-blow. However, of 14 marked carcasses placed on this stretch, the numbers remaining on successive days were 13, 13, 12, 9, 9 and 9. Some of the carcasses present for more than 1 day shifted position during the week, probably mainly by tidal action. On most days, additional carcasses had been washed ashore, namely 21, 9, 5, 3 and 5 and 0, over successive days. Pooling the figures from both weeks, 15 (65%) out of 23 carcasses remained on the beaches for at least a week, the interval between successive searches. These findings showed that our counts could not have included the total numbers of bodies washed ashore each week. Many carcasses were probably carried by tidal action to shorelines elsewhere before they disintegrated, until which time they represented a continually shifting population. Others may have been buried by blowing sand. Because of the small samples, and the unusual conditions during one of the weeks when this work was done, it was unsafe to extrapolate these findings to the whole study period. However, it was reasonable to assume that more carcasses than were counted in weekly searches appeared for a time on the beaches concerned, and that some of the carcasses counted had also spent time on other beaches elsewhere.

## **Transport of floating wooden blocks**

With the likelihood that not all corpses in the sea off Blyth (including some wind-farm victims) would have been washed up in the search area, we decided to

experiment with wooden blocks (cut to the approximate size and weight of a large waterbird, 10 × 10 × 30 cm, 1.5–2.0 kg) dropped into the sea, under the turbines, to find what proportion could be recovered on the local beaches. The two main weather patterns that occurred at Blyth involved south-westerly and north-easterly winds respectively. The hypothesis was that blocks would be most likely to be washed up in the search area when winds blew onto the shore (north-easterly), and that any drift in these conditions would be dependent on the state of the tide. The blocks were uniquely-coded, brightly painted with a florescent stripe on each end according to the release site, and marked with a message, an address and a telephone number. These blocks were released on three different dates on one or other side of each turbine position (river and seaward sides) at both high and low water. In total, some 216 blocks were released in steady south-westerly winds and 108 in steady north-easterly winds. After each release, the study area was searched for four successive days, before reverting to the usual weekly checks.

No significant differences in recovery proportions or locations were found between blocks released at high or low tides, or on the harbour or seaward sides of the turbine wall (in pairwise comparisons, G-test, _P_ > 0.05). However, of the 108 blocks released in easterly winds, 77 (71%) were subsequently found in the search area (all within 4.5 days). A further 12 (11%) were reported by members of the public up to 10 days later on beaches to the south, but still on the eastern side of the country, having travelled distances of up to 280 km (Norfolk) from the release point. Hence, at least 82% of blocks released in easterly winds were found, leaving only 18% unaccounted for.

Of the 216 blocks released in westerly winds, only five (5%) were recovered within the search area, and none were reported from elsewhere in Britain, but 37 (34%) were reported from the opposite side of the North Sea (28 from Denmark, eight from Norway, and one from Sweden), at intervals of 4–217 days later. Hence, a total of 42 (39%) blocks released in westerly winds were recovered and reported, and 74 remained unaccounted for. The difference in proportions recovered in the search area under easterly and westerly winds was highly statistically significant ( χ[2] = 36.6, _P_ < 0.001), as was the difference in proportions reported from the western and eastern sides of the North Sea in different wind conditions ( χ = 104.9, _P_ < 0.001).

These findings therefore confirmed our expectation that blocks released in easterly (onshore) winds were

much more likely to be washed ashore locally than those released in westerly (offshore) winds. Most of the blocks recovered from those released in westerly winds were on shorelines on the opposite side of the North Sea, the first two being reported only 4 days after their release. We assumed that the same could have held for bird carcasses, even though the more elastic properties of carcasses may have slowed their rate of dispersal. A similar experiment with bird carcasses (as carried out by Bibby & Lloyd [1977]) could have produced much lower recovery rates, however, not least because of the scavenging activities of gulls. Another experiment conducted with wooden blocks in Alaska confirmed that many more were washed ashore in onshore than offshore winds (Flint & Fowler 1998).

## **DISCUSSION**

The 3748 bird bodies found during this 11-year study probably represented a large proportion of those washed onto this 4.7 km of shoreline over the 11-year period. While some of these birds had died locally (witness the turbine casualties), others had almost certainly died far away, as they were in an advanced state of decay or entirely skeletal when washed ashore. The several ringed birds found among the carcasses had originated from nesting colonies elsewhere on the coast of eastern Britain, but revealed nothing specific about where they had died. Conversely, not all birds that died locally are likely to have been washed up on local beaches, as they could have been carried elsewhere by currents (as in the ‘block experiments’ described above), especially under westerly winds. The fact that test carcasses stayed afloat for several weeks suggests that carcasses may have been carried long distances before they were washed ashore at Blyth. In this time, they also may have spent periods on other beaches elsewhere, as part of a continually shifting population. Nevertheless, the location at Blyth is likely to have had some influence on the numbers and species composition of bodies found. In particular, the local concentrations of several species around the harbour and estuary are likely to have resulted in larger numbers of fresh carcasses near Blyth than on many other shorelines around Britain. Moreover, the position of the wind-farm, in the midst of the search area, is likely to have resulted in a greater proportion of turbine casualties at Blyth than on most other parts of the British coastline in these years.

The numbers of carcasses washed ashore varied seasonally, and in all years, more appeared in winter than in summer. The numbers also varied more than nine-fold

from winter to winter, with the highest numbers in the coldest winters with more easterly (onshore) winds. Occasional highs were due to particular mortality events in certain species, such as the starvation mortality of Guillemots and Shags in February 1994, and the die-offs of Kittiwakes in the late summers of 1995–97 (attributed on circumstantial evidence to algal toxin poisoning). These various events were evident over a much wider stretch of shoreline than Blyth alone, extending long distances to the north and south.

Overall, the major mortality categories identified were emaciation (mostly starvation, but in some cases perhaps also disease), and predation/scavenging (mostly by large gulls), followed by human-induced causes such as oiling, and entanglement in fishing gear (the latter affecting mainly Guillemots).

Among land-birds, the most common casualties were Pigeons, a reflection perhaps of the large numbers nesting around the harbour, and at cliffs elsewhere on the eastern coasts, and of the large numbers flying up and down the coast on training and racing flights. The Starlings found in winter may have originated from the over-water roost under the wharf in Blyth harbour. Other land-bird species occurred mainly at migration times in spring and autumn, and were assumed to be exhausted or gull-killed migrants. If any small land-birds had been struck by turbine rotors, they may well have been smashed to such an extent that their carcass remains could not have been found or recognized. Beach searches are not appropriate for any small species killed by turbines.

Despite the location of the wind-farm in the midst of the study area, turbine deaths accounted for only 114 (3.04%) of the total carcass remains found in the search area during the 11-year period, about 11.4 birds (or 1.3 birds per turbine) per year of operation. But how many additional birds were killed but not found? Insofar as it is possible to generalize from the experiments that were carried out, the total numbers of birds killed per year by the wind-farm could be estimated. The worst-case estimate is based on the assumptions that: (1) 5% of carcasses present on the beaches during the searches would have remained unfound; (2) up to 35% of corpses would be lost from the beaches between their arrival and the next count; (3) 95% of corpses were lost from the immediate search area under offshore wind conditions and 29% during onshore winds; (4) offshore winds blew on about 59% of the year (as judged from local daily weather records, April 1993– March 1998). On the basis of these assumptions, the maximum likely average annual rate of bird strikes at

Blyth harbour was calculated as 21.5 birds per turbine per year, and as 193.5 birds for the entire nine turbines per year. The greatest error is probably introduced by the assumption that 35% of carcasses were lost from the beaches between searches, because this figure was obtained under rather extreme conditions of tide and wind, and refers to a full week, whereas most carcasses found at each search could have been present for less than a week. If no carcasses had disappeared, the figure would become 16.5 per turbine per year, giving a range of 16.5–21.5 per turbine per year (or 148.5–193.5 for all nine turbines). These figures fall within the range of other figures for coastal onshore wind turbines of similar design which gave mean values of 3.7, 16.6 and 51.1 birds per turbine per year at Kreekrat, Oosterbierum and Urk respectively in the Netherlands (Musters _et al_ . 1996) and of 19.1–20.9 birds per turbine per year (mainly gulls and terns) at Zeebrugge in Belgium (Everaert & Stienen 2007). Other figures for a wider range of turbine designs situated in a wider range of habitats varied from 0 to 60 fatalities per turbine per year, but many estimates were based on corpses found, with no correction for search efficiency or loss from the site (Drewitt & Langston 2008).

Despite the numbers killed, wind-farm casualties at Blyth formed only 3.3% of the 3471 bird carcasses found during the 10 years (1993–2002) when the turbines were operational, suggesting that losses due to the wind-farm were small compared with the overall bird mortality. Most of the casualties were large gulls, drawn from the population of more than 3000 in the harbour area. Scarcity of collisions was supported by 93 hours of daytime observations (conducted in 3-hour sessions through the year) of the behaviour of birds in the vicinity of the wind-farm (Lawrence _et al_ . 2007). In these watches, which were spread over the year, no casualties were observed (the three records being based

on eye-witness accounts outside the routine observation periods). Similarly, no collisions were seen during 177 hours of daytime watches at a different offshore wind-farm nearby (Rothery _et al_ . 2009). However, no observations could be made at either site during periods of darkness or mist when collisions may have been more likely to occur.
